Alger, 12 août 2026 (Algeria Tech) — Goo: Algiers, August 12, 2026 (Algeria Tech) — Google has revised its documentation to explain the technical requirements of its local AI integrated into Chrome and to formalize the deactivation method. The company specifies a minimum disk space of 20 GB for its Gemini Nano model.
Une documentation mise à jour pour justi: Updated documentation to justify technical constraints
Google a discrètement actualisé sa docum: Google quietly updated its support documentation between late July and early August. The company now details the hardware and software prerequisites required to install its local artificial intelligence, Gemini Nano, integrated into the Chrome browser. This AI handles background tasks such as summarizing web pages or detecting scams.
Parmi les exigences les plus notables, C: Among the most notable requirements, Chrome checks that the computer has at least 20 GB of free space before initiating the download of the model, which nevertheless weighs 4 GB once installed. The browser also requires an unlimited internet connection to avoid consuming a mobile data plan in case of tethering. Finally, Chrome ensures that the machine has sufficient processing power to run the AI locally.
Une méthode officielle pour désactiver l: An official method to disable local AI
Face aux critiques des utilisateurs ayan: Faced with criticism from users who attempted to manually delete the AI files, Google is now formalizing the only valid method to disable it. Unlike one-off deletions, Chrome reschedules the automatic download of missing files during the next session. The company therefore recommends using the dedicated option in the browser settings.
Pour ce faire, il convient de se rendre: To do this, users must go to Settings > Chrome System, and then disable the option entitled "Device-on AI". This action triggers an immediate cleanup of downloaded files, disables all associated features, and prevents any future redownloading of the local AI.
Cette mise à jour intervient après les c: This update comes after controversies sparked by Chrome's silent downloads of AI models, notably in May 2026. At the time, many users had discovered with dismay that the browser was occupying 4 GB of storage without prior consent. Google then defended its strategy by citing the benefits of local AI for security and user experience.
